::: {.callout-note .se-question appearance="simple"}
## The question

[Determining the asymptotic growth of a function](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/5112248/determining-the-asymptotic-growth-of-a-function), asked by [Rincewind](https://math.stackexchange.com/users/684300/rincewind) on Mathematics Stack Exchange (2025-12-03; [CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)):

> It's my understanding that $\frac{1}{2^{1/x}-1}=O(x)$ (as $x$ approaches $+\infty$), but I'm struggling to prove why this is the case. How does one prove this?
>
> Thanks!
:::

By L'Hôpital's rule,
$$\begin{aligned}
  \lim_{x\to\infty} \frac{1/(2^{1/x}-1)}{x} 
&= \lim_{x\to\infty} \frac{1/x}{(2^{1/x}-1)}
\\&= \lim_{x\to\infty} \frac{-1/x^2}{(\ln 2)2^{1/x}(-1/x^2)}
\\&= \lim_{x\to\infty} \frac{1}{(\ln 2)2^{1/x}} = \frac{1}{\ln 2}
\end{aligned}$$
